transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well… I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, but I’ve been having a hard time with my husband’s sister. I feel like she’s been working things in the family business so she can get control of the money and sort of push me out of decisions. People keep trying to tell me it’s just misunderstandings or smooth it over, and maybe I don’t explain it right, but I know what I’ve been seeing. It’s been going on for more than a year now.
Aside from your concerns about your sister-in-law, have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people couldn't hear or see?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I don’t hear voices or see things like that. I know how that can sound, and I don’t want you to think I’m making things up or anything. It’s more just… I notice what’s happening with her and the business. But voices or visions, no, not that I’ve noticed.

Aside from your sister-in-law, do you generally find yourself distrustful or suspicious of other people in your life—friends, coworkers, or other family members—or is this feeling really specific to her and the business situation?

I wouldn’t say I’m suspicious of everybody, no. I mean, I still go to my quilting group and choir practice, and I’ve been keeping up with my GED lessons and those senior walks like I always have. So it’s not like I’m shut away or thinking everyone’s against me.

It’s mostly… her, and things around the business. It has made me more careful with my husband’s sister, and I’ve skipped some family get-togethers if I thought it would be uncomfortable. But with other people, I think I’m pretty much the same. Does that make sense?

Before this situation with your sister-in-law started, would you say you generally had a hard time trusting people or often suspected others of trying to deceive or take advantage of you, going back to when you were younger?

I don’t think so… not in a big way. I mean, I’ve always tried to get along with people, and I don’t remember being someone who thought everyone was out to get me or anything like that.

Maybe I could be cautious sometimes, like anybody, but I wouldn’t say it was a pattern. At least, I hope not. Does that answer what you mean?

During this past year while you've been concerned about your sister-in-law, have you also noticed any significant changes in your mood—like feeling persistently sad, hopeless, or unusually elated or full of energy—that lasted for weeks at a time?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I’ve had stressful days, of course, with all this going on, and I can get upset or worried about it. But I wouldn’t say I’ve been sad for weeks and weeks, or suddenly full of energy in some unusual way.

At least, nothing that seemed that extreme to me. Is that the kind of thing you’re asking?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, well-systematized, non-bizarre delusion focused specifically on her sister-in-law's intent to manipulate family business finances and marginalize her from decisions. This belief has persisted for over one year, meeting the duration criterion for delusional disorder. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or behavior, and no evidence of broader pervasive suspiciousness or paranoia extending to other relationships (friends, coworkers, general social circle), which argues against paranoid personality disorder. She denies any sustained mood symptoms (depressive or manic episodes) that would suggest a mood disorder with psychotic features. Functioning outside the circumscribed delusional theme remains largely intact—she continues her quilting group, choir, GED lessons, and walking routine—consistent with delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia, where functional decline and broader psychotic symptoms would be expected. The lack of a lifelong pattern of distrust prior to the current stressor further argues against a personality disorder diagnosis.
